Well, doctor, it’s a bit of a long story, but I’ll try to explain from the beginning. I’ve been working on the production line for years, and they recently asked me to start helping out with the new hire safety trainings. It’s a nice thing to be asked to do, you know, going over the equipment protocols and making sure everyone knows where the emergency shut-offs are. 

But the thing is... ever since I started doing it, I have to stand up there in front of a group and point at the diagrams and the machinery, and I just can’t seem to stop noticing my hands. I look down at them and they just look so terribly wrinkly and... uneven. It's all I can focus on when I’m pointing things out to the new folks. I try to pull my sleeves down or hold my clipboard a certain way to hide them, but you need your hands to train people! 

And then, to make matters worse, it doesn't even stop with my hands. They took some photos recently for the company newsletter to highlight the new safety team. When I saw the pictures, I just couldn't believe it. I started looking at my face in them, and it looks completely crooked. One side just seems totally off-balance and wrong. I've brought it up to a few of the girls at work, and they all swear up and down they don’t see what I’m talking about. They say I look exactly the same as always and that it's just the lighting, but I know what I'm seeing. I just can't stop thinking about how awful it looks, and it's really starting to get to me every time I have to go in and do a training session.

Well, you know, it’s funny you ask that, because it’s definitely worse when I have to be up in front of people, like at the trainings or even if I’m just going to a workshop down at the senior center on the weekends. But it’s not like it just disappears when I’m alone, either. It’s more like a buildup, I guess? I’ll look in the mirror, and I’ll turn my face this way and that way, trying to see if the crookedness is still as bad as I thought, or if maybe I can part my hair differently to hide it. And the hands! Oh, I must put lotion on them three or four times before I leave the house, just hoping it plumps up the skin or smooths out the wrinkles, even though I know it doesn't really do much. I just keep rubbing it in, looking at them under the bathroom light, then the hallway light. And then, when I finally get to work, right before the safety training starts, I’ll usually pull one of the other girls aside—usually Linda, she’s been there forever—and I’ll ask her, "Do I look all right? Is it noticeable?" And she always says I’m fine, but I just have to ask. I mean, all this checking and lotion and asking... it does make me run a little behind schedule sometimes, I admit. I’m always rushing in at the last minute, flustered, but... well, I still get myself there, you know? I haven't missed a training yet, but it’s just this whole routine I have to go through first, just to feel okay enough to walk out the door.

Well, no, I wouldn't say I've completely avoided things. Like I said, I haven't missed a single safety training, and I still go to my shifts on the production line, and I still go down to the senior center to help out with the weekend workshops. I’m very proud of my attendance, honestly. I've always been the type of person who shows up when she says she will, rain or shine.

I just can't bear the thought of seeing my face looking so crooked again, or my hands front and center. 

And, I guess... I do hesitate more before social events. Things I used to really enjoy, like going to lunch with the girls from the line on our days off, or attending the company picnic... I still go, usually, but I really have to talk myself into it now. I’ll stand in my kitchen with my coat on, just agonizing over whether people are going to be staring at my hands while I eat, or if the sunlight at the picnic is going to highlight how uneven my face is. It used to be so easy, you know? I’d just grab my purse and go. Now it’s a whole internal debate, weighing whether it’s worth the stress of feeling so exposed. So, I haven't stopped going, but it’s certainly not as carefree as it used to be. It takes a lot more effort just to get myself out the door and keep a smile on my face once I'm there.

Well, no, it really is just my hands and my face. I mean, I know some women my age—well, my sister, for instance, she’s always going on about her stomach or her thighs, you know, how things shift when you get older. I don't really have the energy to worry about anything else, honestly, because those two things are just so... so glaring to me. But... it's definitely taking a toll, I can't deny that. It's just exhausting, you know? The constant thinking about it. Like I said before, just getting ready to go anywhere has become this whole ordeal with the checking and the lotion and the worrying. It just drains the joy out of things that used to be simple. \n\nLike the company picnic I mentioned earlier. I used to just throw on a nice blouse, make a potato salad, and head out the door looking forward to seeing everyone outside of work. Now, the whole morning leading up to it is just a knot in my stomach. I'm standing there in the kitchen, fussing with my hair, trying to see if it makes my face look less lopsided, rubbing lotion into my hands until they're practically raw, and just dreading the thought of someone noticing how awful I look. By the time I actually get to the park, I'm already so tired from the worrying that it's hard to just relax and enjoy a hot dog, you know? \n\nAnd it's not just the big events, either. It's the little things. It's sitting at a red light on the way home from the plant, and catching a glimpse of my hands on the steering wheel, and suddenly my whole mood just drops. It's like this constant, low-level hum of anxiety in the background of everything I do. It just chips away at you. \n\nSo, yes, I suppose it is interfering. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, that’s the frustrating part of all this, because to me, I really do see them as flawed. I mean, the whole reason I even came in to talk to someone is because of how much I see it myself. 

It really started getting bad when I began helping with the safety trainings at the plant. They asked me to step up because I know the production line so well, which was a nice compliment, but... well, I’m standing up there at the front of the room, and I have to point things out on the whiteboard or hold up the safety gear, and I just can’t seem to stop noticing how wrinkly and uneven my hands look. I’ll be pointing at a chart about lockout-tagout procedures, and the fluorescent lights in that room are just so harsh, and all I can focus on is how old and textured and just... uneven my hands are, right there in front of everyone. I worry the new hires are looking at them, sure, but really, *I'm* the one who can't stop staring at them. I'll lose my train of thought just staring at my own knuckles.

And it's the exact same thing with my face. I really do believe it's crooked. Like I mentioned with those newsletter photos... when Brenda from HR handed me the proof of the safety team spotlight, I almost gasped. My face just looked so lopsided to me, like one side was just pulling entirely differently than the other. But the thing that really gets me going in circles is that when I point it out to people... they say I'm crazy. I showed the picture to my sister, and I even asked Brenda directly, and they both swore up and down that they don’t see it. They said, "Oh, you look fine, you're being ridiculous." 

But how can they not see it? It's right there! They print the newsletter in color now, so it's as clear as day to me. So I start thinking my face looks terribly crooked in the photos, even though other people say they don’t see it at all. It makes me feel like I'm losing my mind a little bit, honestly. Because I know what I'm seeing. I see the wrinkles, I see the unevenness, I see the crookedness. So, yes, I worry about what people think, but mostly because I feel like I'm walking around with these glaring flaws that I just can't fix, no matter what anyone else tells me.

Oh, absolutely. Yes, it's not just about other people at all. I mean, even when I'm completely by myself, the flaws are just as real and just as obvious to me. 

Take a Sunday evening, for example. I live alone, you know, so it's just me in the house. No one is coming over, I'm not going out to the plant or to church or anywhere at all. It's just as lopsided, just as uneven as it is when I'm standing in the breakroom at work with fifty people around. The fact that I'm alone doesn't change what I see in the glass one bit.

And it's the exact same story with my hands. I could be sitting in my recliner in the living room, watching Jeopardy, without a single soul around to judge me or look at me. I'll just be resting my hands in my lap, or maybe holding a warm mug of tea, and I'll glance down and... well, I just see every single wrinkle, every bit of that awful, uneven texture. It doesn't matter that I'm the only one in the room and the curtains are drawn. The flaws are right there. I'll sit there and trace the lines on my knuckles and just feel so upset about how they look, even though nobody else is watching. 

So, it's really not just a matter of being worried about what Brenda from HR thinks, or the new hires on the line. I mean, I do worry about that, like I said, because it's embarrassing to think they're staring at my crooked face or my old-looking hands. But the actual... the actual way they look to me, that doesn't magically get better just because the room is empty. I see it just as clearly. Well... I think... honestly, it’s how they look to me. I really do. Because, and I know I keep coming back to this, but it really is the crux of it all—the whole reason I finally picked up the phone and came in here to see you is because, ever since I started helping with those safety trainings, I just can’t seem to stop noticing how wrinkly and uneven my hands look when I’m up there pointing things out. It’s just this constant, exhausting loop of noticing the flaws, over and over again, and I can't escape it just by closing my front door and being alone.

Like I said, I haven't missed a single safety training, and I still go to my shifts on the production line, and I still go down to the senior center to help out with the weekend workshops. It hasn't stopped me from working or volunteering, but like I mentioned, I am definitely slower getting ready for those trainings. And, well, I have started ducking out of photos. I’ll stand in my kitchen with my coat on, just agonizing over whether people are going to be staring at my hands while I eat, or if the sunlight at the picnic is going to highlight how uneven my face is. It used to be so easy, you know? I’d just grab my purse and go. Now it’s a whole internal debate, weighing whether it’s worth the stress of feeling so exposed. So, I haven't stopped going, but it’s certainly not as carefree as it used to be. It takes a lot more effort just to get myself out the door and keep a smile on my face once I'm there.\n\nDoctor: Is it always your hands and face that you focus on, or do you also worry about other parts of your body?\n\nPatient: Well, no, it really is just my hands and my face. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, I think... when I'm truly alone in my house, I'm really just examining them to see the flaws for myself. I'm trying to see exactly how bad the crookedness is, or just how deep those wrinkles are on that particular day. It's like I have to know the exact extent of the damage, if that makes sense. But I will admit, the whole thing definitely ramps up and gets a bit tangled with other people when I know I actually have to leave the house and be seen. 

Take those safety classes I was telling you about, or even on Thursday evenings—I go to a senior-center workshop, they do a lovely little knitting circle and I really do enjoy it, I've been going for a couple of years now. But getting out the door for any of these things has become such a production. Before a class at the plant or that workshop at the center, I will stand in my bathroom and I’ll check the mirror. And I don't just mean a quick glance to make sure my hair is brushed. I'll check it a few times. I'll stand there and turn my face different ways, tipping my chin up and down, turning side to side, just trying to see exactly how lopsided my face looks from every single angle. 

And my hands, too. I'll stand there at the sink and I'll put lotion on my hands, rubbing it in over and over, just hoping against hope that maybe the moisture will plump up the skin or hide some of that awful, uneven texture before I have to go point at a whiteboard or hold a pair of knitting needles in front of the other ladies. I just get so caught up in examining it all. 

And then, even after all that checking at home, when I get to the plant, I'll still feel so unsettled about it that I’ll sometimes pull a coworker aside—usually Brenda, bless her heart, she really does put up with a lot of my fretting—and I'll ask her if I look all right. I'll ask if my face looks too off-balance today. All of this, the mirror checking and the lotion and the asking... well, it makes me run a little behind schedule, to be honest. I'm always rushing at the last minute, looking at my watch and panicking because I got stuck in the bathroom staring at my own reflection again. But I will say, I still get myself there. I haven't missed a safety training or a workshop yet. I just end up cutting it terribly close because I can't seem to stop examining every little thing before I go.

I really do apologize if I'm just not explaining it right, or if I'm talking in circles—I know I can talk a blue streak sometimes and lose the thread—but it really, truly is just my own dissatisfaction. It’s my own eyes just focusing on the unevenness and the crookedness, and no matter how many times someone tells me I look fine, it doesn't fix the fact that *I* am so terribly unhappy with what I see. I don't spend time looking at my waistline or anything like that. But my hands... well, they're right there in front of me all day.
